title_en: New rail links would bring Asean even closer to China. Will Beijing pay to make it happen?
content_en:
Malaysia, Cambodia and their neighbours eye cheaper freight, but building costs and debt concerns could put the brakes on regional ambitions.
Illustration: Lau Ka-kuen
China and Laos marked a milestone in October, as their joint railway line surpassed 100 billion yuan (US$15 billion) in the cumulative value of imports and exports sent by trains.
A private celebration for the two countries?
Not for long.
Cambodia, Thailand, Malaysia and possibly Vietnam are scoping out ways to link up with the nearly five-year-old China-Laos railway – a move that would cut shipping costs and boost business for Chinese exporters in Southeast Asia, a crucial market as Western countries set up trade obstacles.
That is, if someone can pay for it all.
The four countries are thinking of connecting with the 420km (261-mile) mid-speed railway – which runs from the Laotian capital of Vientiane to the Chinese border – as all have direct or indirect land links to Laos, and to China just north of it.
They also have ties with China on several levels: a buyer of manufactured goods, a seller of factory raw materials, an exporter of consumer electronics and a growing source of tourism.
“There is considerable economic attraction in having direct rail links with China to enable freight and passenger flows to Asia’s largest economy,” said Rajiv Biswas, CEO of Asia-Pacific Economics in Singapore.
“However, a key hurdle for some Asean countries is the commercial feasibility of such high-speed rail links, which have very high infrastructure development costs,” he said, referring to the 11-member Association of Southeast Asian Nations bloc, which includes Cambodia, Laos, Malaysia, Thailand and Vietnam.
Thailand, which shares a long land border with Laos, is already connecting to the railway.
Twelve years ago China and Thailand – a major automotive manufacturing hub that has attracted billions of US dollars in Chinese investment in recent years – agreed to develop rail links, laying the groundwork for a high-speed railway now being built in stages through at least 2031.
An initial 251km (156-mile) section was more than half complete as of August, and the Thai government was planning to take bids for work contracts in December.
In the tourism space, Chinese travellers are expected to make 39.2 million trips to Southeast Asia this year, according to Singapore-based marketing technology company China Trading Desk. It placed Thailand, Vietnam and Malaysia among the largest markets – a function of their low prices and proximity to China.
“Once this rail link connects Thailand and China, it [will offer] considerable economic benefits for fast and efficient bilateral freight shipments as well as boosting bilateral passenger travel,” Biswas said.
China’s trade with wealthier Western countries has hit roadblocks over the years, steering export manufacturers towards Southeast Asia as both a growing market and a production base. Some goods produced there are ultimately sold in Europe and the US.
Despite last year’s de-escalation of ultra-high US import tariffs, Washington has kept hi-tech export barriers in place, while China limits shipments of some critical minerals to the US. In Europe, where trade relations have grown fractious, China and the EU reached a deal in October that caps Chinese hybrid electric vehicle exports.
Asean is China’s largest trading partner and its largest regional export market.
Formally announced in 2015, the China-Laos railway was seen in Laos as a major step in the Southeast Asian country’s push to transition from a landlocked to “land-linked” nation.
Goods trains on the 1,035km (643-mile) China-Laos railway can travel up to 120km/h (75mph). People’s Daily, the official newspaper of China’s ruling Communist Party, said that as of October the railway had given passage to more than 25,000 cross-border goods trains and seen its annual cargo volume grow by over 24 per cent on average.
Rail transport anywhere in the world means fast delivery and much lower fuel costs than other transport methods, the freight forwarder Nissin Belgium has found. It said rail shipping cost up to 80 per cent less than air transport and up to 50 per cent less than road transport.
In May, the China-Laos line began offering a cold-storage rail service linking Thailand with southwest China’s Yunnan province, lowering costs to ship durian – the pungent, spiky fruit beloved by Chinese consumers.
“The China-Laos railway has shown itself to be very much a game-changer,” said independent China railway specialist David Feng.
The fast-growing factory nation of Vietnam, which shares a border with Laos, is proposing a 554km (344-mile) railway between Vientiane and a deep water port in Ha Tinh province, the Lao News Agency reported.
Construction on the US$6.6 billion project was due to start this year towards a launch in 2030, the agency said, “marking a major step towards strengthening regional connectivity and economic integration”.
China has long supplied raw materials to Vietnam’s export manufacturers, with the US Federal Reserve Board calculating the number of firms from mainland China and Hong Kong operating in the country to have risen 122.5 per cent from 2018 to 2023 alone.
Vietnam is known among manufacturers in Asia for cheap labour and a plethora of free-trade deals.
“I think Vietnam for sure wants to be more connected,” Feng said.
Yet officials in Hanoi, wary of Beijing due to long-running territorial and maritime disputes in the South China Sea, remain “very conscious of the leverage China gains” through infrastructure projects linked to its Belt and Road Initiative, said Adam McCarty, chief economist with Mekong Economics in Hanoi.
The China-Laos railway falls under the belt and road, which is aimed at smoothing cross-border trade in much of the world, especially Eurasia.
Proposed railway connections “would be evaluated economically and politically”, McCarty said.
Malaysia has since 2024 run a cross-border goods train service linking Selangor state, just outside the capital, to Chongqing in southwest China via Thailand and Laos. Trips take nine to 14 days, compared with up to three weeks for sea shipments.
The same year, Chinese Premier Li Qiang said his country was open to helping Malaysia turn its domestic East Coast Rail Link project into part of a pan-Asia railway system covering China, Laos, Thailand and possibly other countries.
Simon Chin, founder of Malaysian durian exporter DKing, called the would-be railway linkage “good news for the Malaysian durian industry”, but said that because multiple countries were involved the connections could be difficult.
DKing exports about two tonnes of durians per day during the three-month high season, using pricey air freight for all its fresh produce. The railway as an “alternative” would keep shipping costs down, Chin said.
China takes over 90 per cent of the world’s durian exports.
But the question of who pays construction bills is about as thorny as it gets, analysts said.
The Laotian government’s combined debt exposure to the Export-Import Bank of China for the railway is more than US$1.5 billion – a “considerable sum” compared with the country’s nominal gross domestic product, according to Nick Freeman, associate fellow at Singapore’s ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute.
Overall, Laos owes about half of its external debt to China. The Southeast Asian country received about US$2.8 billion in loan principal deferrals from China between 2020 and 2025, per Fitch Ratings.
A joint venture involving three Chinese state-owned enterprises holds a 70 per cent ownership stake in the China-Laos railway and a Laos state-owned enterprise has the rest, according to the AidData research lab at the US university William & Mary.
Most people in Malaysia would welcome linkages to China’s railways, especially if Chinese investors put up enough money, said Oh Ei Sun, principal adviser at the Pacific Research Centre think tank in Kuala Lumpur.
China is Malaysia’s largest trading partner, with total bilateral trade valued at 542.2 billion ringgit (US$133.6 billion) in 2025.
“The sticky question is who’s going to pay for [railway connections], and of course we hope that China would shoulder the lion’s share of construction costs,” Oh said.
China typically makes investments or offers loans for belt and road projects in poorer countries such as Cambodia and Laos to build relations in the Global South.
But over recent years, China’s belt and road strategy has shifted towards projects it deems “small but beautiful”, undertakings that are easier to finance and less likely to saddle recipient countries with debt.
Railway connections at international borders cost money because one country’s tracks may be narrower than another’s, which can mean tens or hundreds of millions of US dollars in alignment work.
In Cambodia, the minister of public works and transport met counterparts from China and Laos in September to discuss what domestic media outlet the Khmer Times called plans for a direct railway connection.
China is Cambodia’s top source of direct investment and has helped fund major infrastructure as well as commercial projects. The Southeast Asian nation already has US$3.93 billion in public debt outstanding to China, the Khmer Times has said.
But any plans are probably at an early stage and may lack funding, Feng said.
“Funding is the main problem precluding a rail link from Laos to Cambodia being established,” he said. “The main issue is the need – and hence cost – to dig hundreds of kilometres of new track through rugged terrain.
“Whatever the intent, reality reveals we’re merely at the early planning stage,” he said, adding that the will to create the line should be maintained.
By Ralph Jennings

title_en: China’s Persian Gulf oil imports hit high since start of Iran war as producers cut prices
content_en:
October marks fourth straight month of increasing shipments as flow through Strait of Hormuz improves.
Tanks store imported crude oil at Qingdao Port Crude Oil Terminal on April 12 in Qingdao, in eastern China’s Shandong province. Photo: Getty Images
China’s crude oil imports from the Persian Gulf in October surged to their highest monthly volume so far this year as producers offered competitive rates amid conflict-elevated global prices, helping to slow a drawdown in Beijing’s domestic stockpiles.
Shipments from the Gulf region rose 42.4 per cent month on month to 19.7 million tonnes last month, according to the South China Morning Post’s calculation of imports from the seven Gulf countries, excluding Iran, based on Chinese customs data released on Friday. It marked the fourth consecutive month of increase and outpaced September’s 25.6 per cent rise.
Crude from the Gulf accounted for nearly half of China’s total imports in volume terms in October, recovering to around the same share as before the US-Israel war on Iran started at the end of February.
“The increase in China’s October imports was supported by a sharp uptick in Middle Eastern crude availability, especially the recovery in crude flows through the Strait of Hormuz,” said Xu Muyu, principal crude oil analyst at data intelligence firm Kpler.
Flows through the Strait – the vital waterway where shipping had been largely disrupted since the war broke – recovered significantly in September and October, while regional producers also continued efforts to bypass the route, she said.
“Pricing is also a major factor behind the increase in Chinese buying,” Xu said. “With crude availability rising, Middle Eastern producers have been offering competitive prices to attract buying interest.”
Under the status quo, there is still potential for Middle Eastern supply to see further modest growthXu Muyu, oil analyst, Kpler
Global oil prices shot past US$100 per barrel in October following a series of attacks by Yemen’s Houthi militant group on Saudi Arabia. But Saudi oil giant Aramco, as well as other producers, offered discounts to Asian buyers to offset rising freight costs and keep prices competitive.
Rising crude imports helped slow the drawdown in China’s onshore inventories last month – which had hit a record pace in September – before stockpiles began rebuilding this month, Xu said.
Kpler data showed that China’s onshore crude inventories stood at 1.128 billion barrels on October 31, down just over 3 million barrels from the start of October. As of Thursday, inventories had risen to 1.139 billion barrels.
It remained uncertain whether China’s imports would continue to recover, given the persistent risk of escalation in the Strait of Hormuz, Xu said.
“But under the status quo, there is still potential for Middle Eastern supply to see further modest growth,” Xu said.
High freight rates were expected to continue encouraging tankers to transit through the strait despite Iranian strikes, while producers remained incentivised to boost exports for revenue and market share, she added.
China imported 41.9 million tonnes of crude in total last month, the highest level since March, according to customs data. That was 13.2 per cent less than a year earlier, but the value was 40.5 per cent higher.
Shipments from Russia, China’s single biggest foreign supplier of crude oil, rose 10.2 per cent year on year to 10 million tonnes in October, roughly unchanged from September.
By Xinyi Wu

Shipments from the Gulf region rose 42.4 per cent month on month to 19.7 million tonnes last month, according to the South China Morning Post’s calculation of imports from the seven Gulf countries, excluding Iran, based on Chinese customs data released on Friday. It marked the fourth consecutive month of increase and outpaced September’s 25.6 per cent rise.
Crude from the Gulf accounted for nearly half of China’s total imports in volume terms in October, recovering to around the same share as before the US-Israel war on Iran started at the end of February.
“The increase in China’s October imports was supported by a sharp uptick in Middle Eastern crude availability, especially the recovery in crude flows through the Strait of Hormuz,” said Xu Muyu, principal crude oil analyst at data intelligence firm Kpler.
Flows through the Strait – the vital waterway where shipping had been largely disrupted since the war broke – recovered significantly in September and October, while regional producers also continued efforts to bypass the route, she said.
“Pricing is also a major factor behind the increase in Chinese buying,” Xu said. “With crude availability rising, Middle Eastern producers have been offering competitive prices to attract buying interest.”
Under the status quo, there is still potential for Middle Eastern supply to see further modest growthXu Muyu, oil analyst, Kpler
Global oil prices shot past US$100 per barrel in October following a series of attacks by Yemen’s Houthi militant group on Saudi Arabia. But Saudi oil giant Aramco, as well as other producers, offered discounts to Asian buyers to offset rising freight costs and keep prices competitive.
Rising crude imports helped slow the drawdown in China’s onshore inventories last month – which had hit a record pace in September – before stockpiles began rebuilding this month, Xu said.
Kpler data showed that China’s onshore crude inventories stood at 1.128 billion barrels on October 31, down just over 3 million barrels from the start of October. As of Thursday, inventories had risen to 1.139 billion barrels.
It remained uncertain whether China’s imports would continue to recover, given the persistent risk of escalation in the Strait of Hormuz, Xu said.
“But under the status quo, there is still potential for Middle Eastern supply to see further modest growth,” Xu said.
High freight rates were expected to continue encouraging tankers to transit through the strait despite Iranian strikes, while producers remained incentivised to boost exports for revenue and market share, she added.
China imported 41.9 million tonnes of crude in total last month, the highest level since March, according to customs data. That was 13.2 per cent less than a year earlier, but the value was 40.5 per cent higher.
Shipments from Russia, China’s single biggest foreign supplier of crude oil, rose 10.2 per cent year on year to 10 million tonnes in October, roughly unchanged from September.

title_en: China’s university graduates to hit record 13 million in 2027 amid jobs strain
content_en:
Beijing pledges hiring support in advanced manufacturing and modern services, plus retraining for workers at risk of AI displacement.
Job fairs offer graduates a chance to connect with employers as China’s labour market struggles to absorb a growing pool of university degree holders. Photo: China News Service/VCG via Getty Images
The number of Chinese university graduates is expected to hit a record 13 million next summer, adding pressure on a labour market already strained by slowing economic growth.
The 2027 cohort is estimated to be 2.4 per cent larger than this year’s projected 12.7 million graduates, according to the Ministry of Education on Thursday.
China has seen a steady rise in the number of university graduates over the past two decades, following a major expansion of enrolment that began in 1999. The annual number of graduates surpassed 10 million for the first time in 2022 and has continued to climb.
The growing pool of educated workers has helped meet the economy’s rising demand for skilled talent, but the job market is now struggling to absorb the growing number of graduates.
In August, an influx of college graduates pushed the urban youth unemployment rate – which covers people aged 16 to 24 who are not in education – to 18.9 per cent, its highest level since Beijing revised its calculation methodology in 2023.
Also on Thursday, at a national meeting on college graduate employment, officials pledged to make full use of existing policy measures while introducing additional support to ensure “overall employment stability” among university graduates.
Jobseekers crowd a recruitment fair in Chongqing, in China’s southwest, as slowing economic growth puts pressure on the nation’s employment market. Photo: AFP
They also pledged to create more job opportunities in advanced manufacturing and modern services, encourage state-owned companies to expand their workforces, help small and medium-sized businesses hire more workers, and promote entrepreneurship as a source of jobs.
Amid a tough job market, some college students are even willing to pay thousands of yuan for internship opportunities to bolster their résumés and improve their job prospects after graduation.
Others are turning to vocational schools that teach practical skills and promise job opportunities on completion of short courses, as university degrees appear to be losing some of their value in the job market.
As the world’s second-largest economy continues to grapple with slowed growth, weak domestic demand and a faltering property market, the rapid development of AI is adding another layer to anxieties over job displacement.
In response, Beijing issued a guideline late last month aimed at mitigating the impact of AI adoption on jobs. It pledged to “prudently manage the scope, intensity and pace” of AI deployment in labour-intensive industries, and encouraged companies to establish transition periods for workers at risk of displacement.
The guideline also called on employers to give affected workers advance notice of large-scale AI deployment and help them retrain or move into other roles.
By Alice Li

title_en: Fighting AI with AI: how a Chinese cybersecurity giant is defending against new hacks
content_en:
The final part of a three-part series profiles an organisation at the forefront of efforts to balance innovation, safety in China’s AI industry.
An office building of Qi An Xin in Beijing. Photo: Simon Song
Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump met this week in Shenzhen on the sidelines of the Apec meeting, where they discussed introducing shared guard rails on artificial intelligence amid growing numbers of AI-enabled cyber hacking incidents affecting banks and governments worldwide. In the last part of a three-part series profiling Chinese organisations at the forefront of efforts to ensure that innovation does not come at the expense of safety in China’s AI industry, we profile one of China’s biggest cybersecurity firms and outline how it is navigating the agentic AI era.
Qi An Xin Technology Group vice-president Chen Huaping had a lot to say when he stepped onto the stage at a conference organised by China’s public security and cyberspace watchdogs last week in Xiamen, in eastern Fujian province.
Late last month, an Israeli-American cloud security company used the latest AI models to discover critical flaws in PHP, the programming language used by an estimated 70 per cent of websites, causing a surge in hacking attempts.
The incident prompted urgent warnings from Chinese authorities, including the first public vulnerability bulletins published by the national cybersecurity emergency response system since 2021.
Addressing the crowd, Chen revealed that the number of assets affected in China by the PHP discoveries was in the “millions”. AI, he said, was multiplying the cost of leaving known vulnerabilities unpatched by “hundreds or even thousands of times” if they were not fixed immediately.
As one of China’s biggest cybersecurity firms, Qi An Xin has unparalleled insights into China’s sprawling cyberspace. Founded in 2014, the Shanghai-listed company, which has over 5,000 employees, became part of China’s state-backed “national team” for cybersecurity following a landmark investment of roughly 3.73 billion yuan (US$559 million) in 2019 from state-owned China Electronics Corporation.
Its customer base spans some 400,000 major organisations in China, including over 98 per cent of China’s central government departments, centrally administered state-owned enterprises and major banks.
As AI gives malicious actors access to skills once reserved for seasoned hackers, the Beijing-based firm is racing to secure Chinese cyberspace. A major part of its strategy is to leverage AI as a defence. Spearheading those efforts is Gong Yushan, chief executive of the subsidiary through which Qi An Xin operates its AI security business.
According to Gong, the subsidiary focused on two main priorities: using AI to defend its customers and securing the AI systems used by its clients. Both reflect a broader change confronting cybersecurity providers worldwide, as AI ushers in an unprecedented period of cybersecurity challenges while simultaneously representing a possible solution.
“Overall, AI has significantly lowered the barrier to carrying out attacks,” Gong told the South China Morning Post. “It has lowered the level of skill attackers need and raised the operational demands on defenders.”
Gong Yushan, the CEO of Qi An Xin Technology Group in Beijing on Friday. Photo: Simon Song
An evolving threat landscape
The uptick in cyber incidents is mainly because of AI systems’ mastery of coding and software development.
While these capabilities could be used to develop new mobile apps or fix software bugs, some malicious actors were increasingly using AI to automate the exploitation of vulnerabilities. This enabled faster and larger-scale intrusions and compressed the time available for defenders to respond, Qi An Xin’s threat intelligence team said in a midyear report published in August.
For instance, a new unidentified group that emerged this year, which Qi An Xin called “UTG-Q-022”, broke into Chinese routers and VPN devices and stole files, including core design drawings, from an unnamed shipbuilding organisation.
Qi An Xin investigators concluded that the malware was likely generated by AI.
In response, the company has pursued an “All in AI” strategy this year with the AI unit headed by industry veteran Gong at its centre. Before taking up his current role, Gong was head of Qi An Xin’s core in-house research unit Guanxing Laboratory, which specialises in technical work to discover and patch vulnerabilities.
As AI systems have rapidly improved in recent years, the research lab has increasingly turned its attention to stress-testing AI models through simulated attacks.
That shift towards AI is reflected in the company’s broader product line-up, with a range of AI-related products launched or upgraded this year.
These include an AI security operations platform called Aisoc, allowing customers to use the company’s in-house QAX-GPT AI model to assess internal alerts of potential cyber incidents.
According to Gong, the platform could assess the alert in about nine seconds and determine the appropriate response, compared with around five minutes for a human analyst.
These gains in speed compound as AI systems discover increasingly larger numbers of vulnerabilities. In one case shared by the company involving a provincial power-grid customer, Aisoc was able to handle more than 10,000 alerts a day, compared with a human specialist, who could handle an estimated few hundred.
“Security capabilities need to be embedded throughout the AI life cycle,” said Gong.
Other Chinese cybersecurity giants are pursuing similar strategies. Qihoo 360, another “national team” cyber vendor, has ramped up its AI offerings this year to include AI agents that analyse alerts, investigate incidents and detect phishing emails.
Meanwhile, Shenzhen-based Sangfor Technologies’ similarly named Sangfor Security GPT products also automate threat analysis and help security teams filter false alarms.
For Qi An Xin, there were early signs that its new products were gaining traction. In a November research note, Huatai Securities analysts described Qi An Xin’s AI products as moving from pilot projects towards larger-scale deployment. They cited AI-related orders exceeding 50 million yuan in the first nine months, up 223 per cent from a year earlier, including more than 35 million yuan for Aisoc.
The brokerage maintained its “buy” recommendation, while flagging government spending pressures and intensifying competition, including from 360 and Sangfor. Revenue for the company was 2.27 billion yuan for the first nine months of the year, down 20.2 per cent, according to its latest quarterly filing.
The Tiger Tally, the logo of Qi An Xin, is pictured in Beijing. Photo: Simon Song
Closing the gap
According to Gong, one of the biggest issues was getting Chinese companies and institutions to take cybersecurity seriously. There was generally lower willingness to pay for software products in China, with its software-as-a-service market far smaller than that of the US.
According to US cybersecurity firm Censys, as of Friday, China had patched 5.8 per cent of PHP vulnerabilities since they were discovered. In contrast, the US had patched 33.9 per cent.
However, there is heightened attention on whether new entrants in China’s cybersecurity market could provide a boost to the industry. One of these is Beijing-based AI model developer Z.ai, also known as Zhipu AI, which in recent months has advertised its GLM models’ ability to discover software vulnerabilities.
In August, the Hong Kong-listed company launched an open-source initiative that offered free security audits to help users patch software vulnerabilities, as well as automated code-auditing tools via its ZCode platform.
A growing debate, however, was whether the open-source ecosystem – advocated for by firms like Z.ai – was a net positive for cybersecurity in China. Some experts have warned that open-weight models could allow malicious actors to more easily conduct cyberattacks. Meanwhile, its supporters said that open models could help shore up cyberspace by proliferating the cyber defensive capabilities of AI systems more widely.
For Gong, while open models have their benefits, his company was seeing rapid acceleration in how quickly vulnerabilities were being exploited “on an hourly basis” due to automated attacks.
The number of vulnerabilities discovered by the company in the first half of the year had increased by 51.9 per cent year on year, with 30.2 per cent of the most high-risk vulnerabilities exploited on the day of their discovery.
Earlier this month, Qi An Xin researchers noted that an unspecified hacker used a jailbroken DeepSeek open model to attempt to breach a dozen organisations, including a European telecommunications provider. DeepSeek did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
According to Gong, the situation was placing greater pressure on defenders than attackers in the near term, though it remains to be seen whether open-weight models could be harnessed to better help defenders in the long term.
“If defences cannot evolve as quickly as attacks, openness itself will become a source of risk,” he said.
By Minxiao Chang

title_en: Oman’s rising commercial ties with China revive the Zheng He spirit
content_en:
With the aid of IFC Oman, Muscat’s partnership with Beijing is evolving and helping Chinese firms turn connections into lasting ventures.
Wind turbines made by Goldwind are loaded onto a ship for export to Oman at the port in Lianyungang, Jiangsu province, on November 5. Photo: AFP
Visitors walking along the beach in Salalah who make a short detour inland will come across a white monument in the shape of a sail set among undulating waves. It commemorates Zheng He, the Chinese explorer who travelled to Oman on behalf of the Ming dynasty in the 15th century.
Erected in 2023, the monument recalls the journeys Chinese sailors made centuries ago to foster relations with Oman. That exchange continues to evolve: our recent discussions in Beijing focused on advanced technologies, far removed from the silk, spice and porcelain trade of yesteryear.
Oman began exporting oil to China in 1983, becoming the first Arab nation to do so directly. Omani energy has since helped power China’s economic growth. Now, that partnership is broadening, with Chinese technology and expertise helping advance Oman’s own diversification drive. Trade between Oman and China has flourished, with goods trade between the two and reaching US$32.8 billion in 2025.
IFC Oman, the new financial centre in Muscat, will be part of the evolution of our economic relationship, helping Chinese businesses establish operations and build long-term partnerships in the Sultanate of Oman. It will connect their capabilities with Oman’s ambition for a more diverse economy, building on the strong foundations of our energy trade.
There are significant opportunities for Chinese businesses and investors. Oman has already attracted substantial foreign direct investment (FDI), reaching 31.4 billion Omani rials (US$81.7 billion) by the end of 2025. Oil and gas extraction drew 80 per cent of that FDI, compared with around 8.5 per cent in manufacturing and around 4.8 per cent in financial intermediation.
There is considerable scope for building on this success. Chinese businesses can help expand Oman’s economic base, particularly in manufacturing and technology.
President Xi Jinping and Oman’s Sultan Haitham bin Tariq attend a welcoming ceremony during the sultan’s state visit to China at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing on November 2. Photo: EPA
As a member of IFC Oman’s board, I see the centre’s role as making this shift practical for businesses. We will provide a predictable legal and regulatory framework, giving firms the foundations to establish operations and grow over the long term.
The benefits must work for both sides. For Oman, new ventures and knowledge-sharing can support economic diversification. For Chinese businesses, IFC Oman is intended to offer a base for seizing the investment opportunities in the sultanate and to serve neighbouring markets.
Oman’s ports, free zones and industrial networks provide a strong commercial foundation, already connecting businesses with international markets across the Gulf, Asia and Africa. Sohar Port alone handled 52 million metric tons (57.3 tons) of cargo in the first half of 2026, up 52 per cent year on year. Container throughput rose 40 per cent to 545,000 twenty-foot equivalent units. IFC Oman is intended to complement this infrastructure by providing access to the financial services which businesses need to develop their projects.
Recent agreements signed in Beijing, covering areas including artificial intelligence and the digital economy, reflect the relationship’s evolving scope. This broader cooperation is already evident in projects across Oman.
A Chinese partner began construction of a US$1 billion manufacturing plant in Sohar in May, while an agreement between Asyad Group and JD.com envisages distribution facilities in Oman serving markets across the Gulf and East Africa.
[embedded media]
Projects of this kind address the requirements of Chinese companies seeking to establish operations in Oman: financing, specialist advice, corporate structures and local partnerships. IFC Oman is intended to bring these services and institutions together, supporting businesses wishing to establish and expand their operations in our country.
Chinese businesses need predictable rules, reliable contract enforcement and clear dispute resolution alongside market access. In the coming weeks, IFC Oman will set out its legal and regulatory framework. This will help give Chinese firms greater confidence to make long-term commitments in Oman while supporting the centre’s contribution to the Sultanate’s economic diversification.
Oman’s five-year plan targets 5.9 per cent growth in manufacturing, 10.8 per cent in the digital economy and 7 per cent in transport and logistics, with the goal of raising FDI inflows to 11 per cent of GDP. These are areas where Chinese businesses already excel and bring deep sector experience. IFC Oman will help facilitate greater investment in these sectors.
In Salalah, Chinese companies have invested in the Salalah Free Zone. Across Oman, Chinese direct investment stood at more than 900 million rials in the first half of this year, while bilateral trade reached 9.6 billion rials in 2025.
The ships that once crossed the Indian Ocean carried the goods of their age; today, technology and capital accompany the trade between our countries. IFC Oman’s task is to help businesses turn those connections into lasting ventures. The monument to Zheng He on Salalah’s shoreline recalls that shared history, but the commercial relationship it represents shows how much opportunity there is still to harness.
By Abdulsalam bin Mohammed Al Murshidi

title_en: The subtle symbolism behind the silk scarves worn by the Apec leaders at Shenzhen summit
content_en:
The seemingly simple items of clothing incorporated a number of traditional techniques and designs as well as a message of unity.
Apec leaders pose for a group photo in the specially made scarves. Photo: Sam Tsang
When Apec leaders assembled in Shenzhen on Thursday for their group photo, they kept up one of the bloc’s traditions by donning traditional garb from the host country.
This time, rather than the more elaborate outfits worn at some previous summits – including the “new Chinese-style” jackets worn the last time China hosted the event – the leaders just slipped on an understated silk scarf over their formal clothing.
In keeping with China’s meticulous approach to major international gatherings, this seemingly simple choice was the result of careful, behind-the-scenes work by the designers and artisans who made them.
Each scarf has 21 threads of wild silk woven into the fabric to represent close, mutually beneficial cooperation among Apec’s 21 member economies, according to Wu Jianhua, chairman of its lead designer, the Suzhou Shangjiukai Silk Technology and Culture Company.
Wu told state news agency Xinhua that the firm hoped that when the leaders put on the scarf put they would “feel not only the depth of Chinese culture, but also a sense of an Asia-Pacific community”.
Wu also took charge of designing the fabric used in the jackets worn by the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation leaders in Beijing in 2014 that incorporated design elements from several dynasties.
China’s last Apec summit, in 2014, saw the leaders wearing “new Chinese-style jackets”. Photo: Reuters
Leaders attending the Shenzhen Apec summit were given two options to wear – a deep red and a deep blue, the colours of the Apec emblem – each decorated using two separate traditional embroidery techniques and in muted tones designed to pair easily with formal wear.
The red version was crafted from gambiered Guangdong silk, also known as xiangyunsha, or fragrant cloud silk.
Wu told Beijing Daily that because the Guangdong gauze was dyed using extracts from the gambier plant, it was notoriously difficult to achieve a consistent hue, prompting artisans to run more than 300 test samples to ensure colour uniformity.
On the tips, one side was embroidered with golden auspicious clouds – one of the oldest and best-known Chinese decorative motifs – and rolling waves, while the reverse featured the Apec emblem in reddish-orange.
In Chinese culture, cloud and wave motifs symbolise good fortune, peace and enduring prosperity.
The blue version is woven from Song brocade, featuring silver cloud and wave patterns on one side and a blue-green emblem on the other.
The traditional silk fabric dates back to the Song dynasty (960–1279) and is inscribed on Unesco’s Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.
The scarves featured a range of traditional motifs, with waves and clouds symbolising good fortune, peace and properity. Photo: qq.com
The dyeing and finishing techniques for gambiered Guangdong gauze are also recognised as part of China’s national intangible cultural heritage, as are the Guangdong and Suzhou embroidery techniques used on the patterns.
Guangdong is the province where Shenzhen is located, while Suzhou is a city long famed for its silk and needlework.
Beyond the main motifs at either tip, the scarf’s subtle background pattern weaves together three elements: kapok blossoms, bougainvillea and auspicious clouds.
Known locally as the “hero flower”, kapok has become a symbol of the pioneering spirit of the Greater Bay Area, while bougainvillea is the official city flower of Shenzhen.
By Carol Yang

title_en: ‘If there is doubt, shoot’: why a Malaysian police order has critics on edge
content_en:
Experts warn the Kuala Lumpur police chief’s audio lowers the bar for lethal force, citing missing bodycams and 327 killings over 10 years.
Kuala Lumpur police chief Fadil Marsus speaks at a press briefing. An earlier audio message in which he urged officers to fire without hesitation when facing threats has sparked debate over the use of deadly force. Photo: Facebook/Polis KL
A Malaysian police chief’s order for officers to fire without hesitation when facing threats has sparked debate over the use of deadly force, following three fatal police shootings since last week, including a machete attack that severed an officer’s hand.
The directive by Kuala Lumpur police chief Fadil Marsus came after a foreign national wielding two machetes was shot by police and was pronounced dead upon arrival at hospital last Wednesday. The suspect had allegedly severed the right hand of an officer responding to reports of a man running amok at an apartment complex in the capital’s Kepong district.
“Take out your weapon, ready, cock [your guns], shoot if there are any obstacles. If there is doubt, shoot. If you are worried, shoot; if there is a threat, shoot. Don’t wait,” Fadil said in an audio message posted last Thursday on the Kuala Lumpur police’s Facebook page.
Malaysia’s national police headquarters subsequently said the injured officer had refrained from opening fire during the confrontation out of concern for the safety of bystanders.
While police officers have the right to defend themselves against life-threatening attacks, criminologists and rights activists warned that Fadil’s directive could encourage the use of firearms in situations where less drastic action might be adequate.
The Kepong incident was one of three fatal shootings involving police since last week. A suspected serial robber was killed in a shoot-out in central Kuala Lumpur on Wednesday, while another man was shot dead in a gunfight in neighbouring Perak state a day later.
Police officers are entitled to protect themselves because their lives “matter just as much as anyone else”, criminologist Shamir Rajadurai said.
But he stressed that firearms should only be used when there is a direct and immediate threat of death or serious injury with no safer way to protect those at risk.
“The directive should be to protect life. We don’t want to risk giving officers the impression that the slightest incident is enough to open fire,” said Shamir, founder of crime prevention consultancy Prevent Crime Now.
Questions over the use of lethal force by Malaysian police have surfaced repeatedly in recent years, including in cases that have led to court proceedings and calls for greater accountability.
Malaysian police officers stand guard during a demonstration in Kuala Lumpur in October 2025. Photo: AFP
The courts have yet to set a date for an inquest into the deaths of three men during a confrontation with police in the rural town of Durian Tunggal, in the southern state of Melaka, last November. The men, aged between 24 and 29, were shot dead after one of them seriously injured an officer during the predawn incident at an oil palm plantation.
In a written parliamentary reply earlier this month, Home Minister Saifuddin Nasution Ismail said authorities had needed time to complete an in-depth investigation into the case.
“The government wishes to stress that the inquest proceedings have not been deliberately delayed,” Saifuddin said, adding that the police force would extend its full cooperation to the court.
In 2021, a high court in Kuala Lumpur ordered police to pay more than 1.5 million ringgit (US$364,700) in damages to the families of three men shot dead by police in 2010 – an award the Court of Appeal later reduced to 630,000 ringgit (US$153,150) in 2023 while upholding police liability. The families had alleged that the men, who police accused of belonging to a robbery gang, were killed execution-style.
In a separate case, a 15-year-old boy was killed at the end of a late-night car chase in 2010 after an officer fired more than 20 shots at his vehicle in a residential area of Shah Alam, the capital of Selangor state. The High Court awarded more than 400,000 ringgit in damages to the teenager’s family in 2016 after finding the police negligent.
In February, Saifuddin told parliament that police had shot dead 327 people across 193 incidents between 2015 and 2025, adding that those killed included suspected criminals and individuals who had attacked officers with dangerous weapons.
A common thread running through many past cases was that they happened in secluded areas at odd hours, leaving little independent evidence to challenge police accounts that those killed posed a threat, said social activist S Arutchelvan.
Arutchelvan, who is also deputy chairman of the Malaysian Socialist Party, said there was no indication that officers involved in recent shootings were wearing body cameras, despite a 2024 government mandate requiring them as part of standard duty gear.
He added that the government should make inquests mandatory for every fatal police shooting, similar to an existing requirement for deaths in custody.
“When anyone is shot dead by the police, they should have an inquiry to establish how the person was killed,” he said.
By Joseph Sipalan

title_en: Xi urges China-Singapore innovation partnership in talks with PM Lawrence Wong
content_en:
Chinese leader also calls the two countries ‘friendly close neighbours’ that should deepen their strategic communication.
Singaporean Prime Minister Lawrence Wong (left) and Chinese President Xi Jinping held bilateral talks in Shenzhen on Friday after the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation leaders' meeting. Photo: MDDI Singapore
Chinese President Xi Jinping encouraged China and Singapore to be “development partners that lead in innovation”, urging closer coordination within regional groupings such as the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean).
In talks with Singaporean Prime Minister Lawrence Wong on Friday, Xi called the countries “friendly close neighbours” that should deepen strategic communication and strengthen solidarity, according to mainland state news agency Xinhua.
“China and Singapore should be sincere friends who trust each other,” Xi said.
“They should be development partners that lead in innovation,” he added, saying the two should deliver results in areas ranging from the digital economy to artificial intelligence. He also called for the launch of talks to upgrade their free- trade agreement.
[embedded media]
A statement from Singapore’s foreign affairs ministry said the two leaders hailed the “excellent state” of ties and agreed to work together on “new areas”.
Talks to upgrade their free-trade agreement would help the two sides strengthen cooperation in AI and innovation and open up new markets, it added.
The ministry said Singapore would join the Group of Friends for the Global Governance Initiative, a China-led grouping at the UN that promotes Xi’s push to reshape international institutions.
Xi and Wong held talks after the conclusion of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in the Chinese coastal city of Shenzhen.
Wong is on a four-day working visit to China that was to include Beijing on Friday and Saturday.
Xi also said China and Singapore should be “progressive forces upholding international fairness and justice”.
This meant stepping up coordination within multilateral frameworks such as the Apec forum and the China-Asean mechanism to “keep East Asian cooperation on the right course” and safeguard regional peace and stability.
Southeast Asia has increasingly found itself caught in the middle of the great-power rivalry between Washington and Beijing. Most countries in the region have deep trade ties with China and have long insisted they would not take sides.
For more than a decade before 2025, China was Singapore’s largest trading partner, while the city state has maintained close security ties with the US.
Singapore is a founding member of Pax Silica, a US-led initiative to secure supply chains for AI, chips and critical minerals amid Washington’s growing tech rivalry with Beijing. It has not joined the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organisation (Waico), widely seen as China’s answer to the US effort.
Singaporean Prime Minister Lawrence Wong’s meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping was his third as prime minister and came on his second trip to China this year. Photo: AFP
Days earlier, Wong said he had a “good conversation” with US President Donald Trump at a US-Asean summit held in the Philippine capital of Manila.
“I told him … all of us appreciate his personal commitment to engaging Asean and being present at our Asean meetings,” Wong said, referring to Trump and the regional bloc. “It speaks to also the fact that America is a Pacific power.”
“We want America to continue to engage Southeast Asia. We value the Americans’ presence here in this part of the world and the fact that the American president takes this commitment seriously … I think that’s good for Asia, good for Southeast Asia.”
Wong’s meeting with Xi was his third as prime minister and came on his second trip to China this year.
The two leaders met on the sidelines of the Apec gathering in Peru in November 2024 before Wong made his first official visit to China in June last year, meeting Xi in Beijing to mark the 35th anniversary of Sino-Singaporean diplomatic relations.
During that meeting, Xi called for the two Asian countries to deepen cooperation and mutual trust, as well as support each other’s core interests.
He said Beijing was ready to work with Singapore to “stand on the right side of history” and advocate for an equal and orderly multipolar world.
In March, Wong visited China for the Boao Forum for Asia in Hainan. There, he delivered a keynote speech calling for China to play a bigger role in supporting regional stability and prosperity.
Friday’s meeting came as Singapore-based cloud computing firm Megaspeed faces renewed scrutiny over a reported diversion of restricted Nvidia chips to China.
American authorities this week said the US Justice Department was conducting a criminal investigation into Megaspeed.
Singapore’s home affairs ministry last week said police investigations into the firm and six individuals were continuing.

title_en: 11-second handshake: Takaichi adopts more proactive approach with Xi at Apec, experts say
content_en:
Behavioural analysts examine Japanese prime minister’s non-verbal cues with China’s president during Apec summit.
Sanae Takaichi walks past Xi Jinping after they shook hands and before a group photo is taken during the Apec Summit in Shenzhen on Thursday. Photo: EPA
Exchanges between top Chinese and Japanese leaders show Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi adopting a far more proactive approach to assert control and seek direct communication, according to body language experts.
Over the past two days, the Apec gala in Shenzhen has been the scene of rare in-person, high-level interactions between the two countries’ leaders, the most notable since ties between Beijing and Tokyo became severely strained over Takaichi’s remarks regarding Taiwan in November last year.
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi shakes hands with China’s President Xi Jinping before the welcome banquet on Wednesday. Photo: Pool via Reuters
Ahead of the welcome banquet on Wednesday evening, Chinese President Xi Jinping and his wife Peng Liyuan each briefly shook Takaichi’s hand before the three posed for photos.
Takaichi appeared to say a few words to Xi during the handshake, but Xi did not say anything or nod, according to videos online. The handshake between Takaichi and Peng was also brief and without visible verbal communication.
Online footage showed Takaichi spreading both hands near her hips, palms partially upturned, immediately after shaking hands with Xi.
Geoff Beattie, a psychology professor at Edge Hill University in Britain, said Takaichi’s low open-palm gesture indicated the Japanese leader’s “uncertainty and discomfort” after that brief handshake, which he described as “formal and cursory”.
However, body language expert Leow Chee Seng highlighted Takaichi’s bearing, including her already-extended arms as she approached Xi, the slight inclination of her upper body towards the Chinese leader, and the way she faced him directly.
“Open palms do not reliably indicate a person’s status, confidence or true intentions,” said Leow, co-founder of the Malaysia-based behavioural intelligence organisation, Humanology.
“Takaichi’s most distinctive behaviour is her repeated initiative,” he said, adding that the pattern was consistent and became even more explicit during their interactions on the second day of the summit.
[embedded media]
The two leaders’ exchange on Thursday – just before world leaders posed for the summit’s family photo – raised even more eyebrows, with Takaichi shaking Xi’s hand for about 11 seconds, significantly longer than other leaders.
During the handshake, Takaichi spoke a few words to Xi, according to online footage. The Chinese leader nodded slightly and smiled, without appearing to say anything in reply.

On Thursday, the ministry said that as host, China had made “appropriate” protocol arrangements for all participating parties in accordance with international practice.

Beijing regards Taiwan as part of China and has never renounced the use of force to bring it under its control. title_en: Xi Jinping urges trust-based partnership with Australia in Shenzhen bilateral talks
content_en:
The Australian prime minister said Canberra was ready to strengthen cooperation in trade, investment and AI.
Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and President Xi Jinping ahead of their meeting in Shenzhen on Friday. Photo: EPA
China and Australia should be “partners that trust each other”, President Xi Jinping told Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese in Shenzhen on Friday.
Xi struck an upbeat tone on Beijing’s relationship with Canberra, describing it as “developing steadily” now, in the meeting after the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation leaders’ summit in the southern Chinese city.
“China and Australia have neither historical grievances nor fundamental conflicts of interest, and should be partners who trust each other and help each other succeed,” the Chinese leader said, according to the official Xinhua news agency.
He called for the two countries to continue working together in agriculture, energy and minerals, while expanding cooperation in the green economy, renewables, digital industries, artificial intelligence and climate change.
Albanese, who was making his third visit to China while in office and sitting down with Xi for the fifth time, echoed that Canberra was ready to deepen high-level exchanges with Beijing while strengthening cooperation in trade, investment and AI.
He also told Xi that Australia was willing to make its relationship with China a model for constructive ties between countries with different political systems, according to the Chinese readout.
The Australian delegation, led by Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, attends a meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen on Friday. Photo: Reuters
Addressing a press conference on Friday after the bilateral meeting, Albanese characterised his exchange with Xi as “constructive, friendly and engaging in the mutual interests of both Australia and China”.
“It is important that Australia continue to engage in a constructive way with China, manage our differences, but not be defined by them,” he said.
According to Xinhua, Albanese framed China as an important stabilising force in a turbulent world and congratulated Xi on hosting the historic three-way summit with US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday.
Speaking to reporters, the Australian leader on Friday described the three countries’ joint declaration towards peace as “positive”, adding that it was “always better to have dialogue than to have conflict”.
This week’s trip to China – his first since July last year – came as Albanese’s Labour government continued its efforts to keep Australia’s ties with its largest trading partner on a stable footing since the end of nearly four and a half years of trade conflict in 2024.
Also on Friday, he will attend the annual bilateral leaders’ meeting with Chinese Premier Li Qiang in Beijing and meet Zhao Leji, China’s third-ranking official who heads the country’s top legislature.
Albanese’s latest encounter with Xi built on a flurry of ministerial engagements between the two countries, including separate visits to China earlier this month by the assistant minister for foreign affairs and trade Matt Thistlethwaite and agriculture minister Julie Collins.
Yet bilateral ties have remained tense in the security and defence domains.
Before heading for the Apec conference, Albanese joined US President Donald Trump, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Japan’s Sanae Takaichi in Manila on Tuesday for the first Quad summit in more than two years.
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, India’s Narendra Modi, US President Donald Trump and Australia’s Anthony Albanese ahead of the Quad leaders’ meeting in Manila on Tuesday. Photo: EPA
With the Trump administration shifting US foreign-policy priorities and pressing allies for more burden sharing, Australia has stepped up to weave its own security web in the region.
Canberra has strengthened bonds with Japan and the Philippines, signing a defence cooperation arrangement with Manila on November 15 and a warship megadeal with Tokyo in April.
While increasing its presence in the disputed South China Sea in recent years, Canberra is also competing with Beijing for influence across the Pacific nations.
Australian defence minister Richard Marles has repeatedly accused China of undertaking the world’s biggest conventional military build-up since World War II without transparency or strategic reassurance.
He renewed that criticism last month, prompting a rebuke from Beijing.
As Washington pushes to build a critical minerals supply chain less dependent on China, resource-rich Australia’s strategic standing has grown more pronounced, prompting experts in Beijing to warn of mounting competitive pressures over the medium to long term.
Australia on Monday joined the US-led San Francisco Declaration to keep AI supply chains from dependence on China.
Security tensions appear to have been casting a shadow over economic and educational ties, with the Australian government’s repeated intervention in 2026 to force some China-linked investors out of rare earths company Northern Minerals.
The actions, on national security grounds, extend a multi-year saga. The Australian federal government has previously voiced concerns about potential Chinese control over supplies to make military hardware, satellites and electric motors.
[embedded media]
Canberra has also signalled that it remains committed to restoring Australian control of Darwin Port, leased to China’s Landbridge Group under a 99-year agreement signed in 2015.
During the press conference on Friday, Albanese was asked about his previous public remarks that China was seeking hegemony, at least over the longer term in the region.
“We have different political systems, different histories, but that doesn’t mean that you can’t have constructive dialogue and that’s what Australia seeks,” he responded.
In an article published on Thursday in The Australian newspaper, China’s top envoy to Canberra, Liu Jinsong, warned that the bilateral relationship was “at a crossroads – pressure to fall back on one side, momentum to move forward on the other”.
Liu called on the two economically “natural partners” to expand “frontier cooperation in artificial intelligence, biotechnology and clean energy”.
China has been Australia’s largest export market and import source for 17 consecutive years.
In US dollar terms, China’s imports from Australia grew by 40.9 per cent from a year earlier in the first 10 months of 2026, while exports to the South Pacific country were up 20.8 per cent, according to Chinese customs data.
By Orange Wang

title_en: No fowl play: Singapore judge throws out passenger lawsuit after driver stops for chicken
content_en:
The claimant alleged negligence but the district judge called it ‘the vicissitudes of life’, noting she had two other accident cases pending.
A rooster walks across a paved surface. A Singapore district judge dismissed a passenger’s negligence lawsuit after her private-hire driver braked suddenly to avoid a bird crossing in front of the car ahead. Photo: Shutterstock
For one Singaporean woman, it did not matter why the chicken crossed the road – only that it did, and caused her harm. She sued her private-hire car driver for braking suddenly to avoid the bird, which she said threw her violently forward.
The judge, however, dismissed the claim as part of “the vicissitudes of life” and ordered her to pay S$15,000 (US$11,600) in legal costs, The Straits Times reported. “This was a trial that arose because a chicken crossed the road,” District Judge Jonathan Ng wrote in his grounds of decision on Wednesday. Chen has since filed an appeal to the High Court.
According to the suit, the claimant, Yvonne Chen, was in a private-hire vehicle driven by Tan Teng Kiat along Holland Road on February 19, 2024, when the bird – which she described as a junglefowl while Tan called it a rooster – crossed the path of the car in front of them, CNA reported.
The vehicle ahead made an emergency stop to spare the bird, causing Tan to brake hard to avoid a crash.
Chen sued Tan for negligence, alleging that his “abrupt and forceful stop” was a result of tailgating the car in front. As everything happened in a “split second”, she had no time to anticipate the stop or brace herself, she told the court, resulting in injuries that were not detailed in the suit.
Tan, however, said he was driving at about 50km/h (31mph) at the time and was roughly 10 metres (33ft) behind the first car.
Singapore’s highway code requires motorists to keep at least one car length behind the vehicle ahead for every 16km/h of speed. At 50km/h, that is roughly three car lengths, or 12 to 15 metres.
However, Ng said he did not need to determine whether Tan’s distance was adequate, as the driver managed to stop in time without hitting the vehicle ahead.
There was nothing more Tan could reasonably have been expected to do, as it was unlikely that either driver would have had the luxury of time to brake normally, he added. “It would have been wholly unrealistic to expect the defendant to have applied a ‘normal’ brake in view of the suddenness with which the sequence of events unfolded.”
Ng also noted that Chen had at least two other accident suits pending before the District Court. In both cases, she was a passenger in either a private-hire vehicle or her husband’s car.
While acknowledging that she was “an innocent passenger” who was injured in an incident beyond her control, the judge said the law did not require someone to be held responsible for every misfortune suffered by another person.
“In an imperfect world, some losses must lie where they fall,” he wrote. “This incident, caused as it was by a chicken crossing the road, was unfortunately, but also undoubtedly, part of the vicissitudes of life.”
It is not known what happened to the chicken.
Free-ranging chickens and native red junglefowl are commonly spotted across Singapore. Over the past five years, there had been an average of about 2,000 instances of public feedback a year involving free-ranging chickens in residential estates, the Ministry of National Development said in a written reply to parliament on January 14.

title_en: China’s battery-powered heavy trucks see electric growth
content_en:
Fast-evolving battery and charging technologies have given electric heavy trucks the lead in China, fostering decarbonisation and leaving Europe and the US far behind.
On a recent 5,000-kilometre journey by battery-electric heavy truck in China, Ceva Logistics slashed energy costs by 43 per cent compared with using a diesel-powered equivalent.
The French company’s economical road trip from Shenzhen in the country’s south to Alashankou in the far northwest, which involved nine recharging stops, is evidence of China’s rapidly growing lead in the development of new-energy articulated lorries, 18-wheelers and industrial vehicles and the infrastructure to support them.
By the end of this year, nearly one in twelve of the 8 million-plus heavy trucks that each year carry 40 billion tonnes of freight on China’s roads, move coal around mines and shuttle goods at ports will be powered by alternative energy. (In China a heavy truck or HGV is one that, when fully loaded, weighs at least 11 tonnes.)
Sales of new-energy heavy goods vehicles (HGVs) in China – including small numbers of plug-in hybrids and those powered by hydrogen fuel cells – have risen rapidly in 2026. The growth has been driven as much by fast-evolving technology, the buildout of supporting infrastructure and lower running costs as by rising diesel prices from the US-Israeli war on Iran, a major oil supplier to the country, industry figures say.
In September, new-energy heavy-truck registrations in China surpassed 50 per cent for the second time in less than a year. More than 99 per cent of these were battery-electric models. The trend continued in October, with electric heavy trucks accounting for 57 per cent of registrations, up from 29 per cent a year earlier, according to trade magazine Commercial Vehicle News – putting China streets ahead of Europe and North America.
“In the heavy-truck electrification market, the competition between internal combustion and electric vehicles is already over; from now on, the competition will be between EV technologies and business models,” the world’s biggest battery maker, Ningde, Fujian-based Contemporary Amperex Technology (CATL), said, according to an October report by Chosun Biz, a South Korean business news website.
Heading for a 100 per cent electric fleet
Long before the Iran war, battery-electric trucks were shown to be more cost-effective than diesel-fuelled ones if used intensively.
In 2024, Shenzhen Xieli New Energy and Intelligent Connected Vehicle Innovation Centre, a think tank based in Shenzhen, Guangdong, conducted a pilot programme which showed electric models beat their diesel rivals in terms of total cost of ownership – lifetime direct and indirect costs – once annual mileage exceeds 60,000 kilometres (37,300 miles). Meanwhile, business magazine Caijing reports that running a new-energy HGV over 10 years costs 1.2 million yuan less than a conventional-fuel HGV.
The national HGV fleet would one day be almost entirely battery electric, Changsha, Hunan-based manufacturer Sany Truck’s chairman, Liang Linhe, predicted at an industry forum in April. That is despite a current price tag per vehicle up to 450,000 yuan (US$67,400) higher than for a diesel equivalent, according to online news portal Sohu.
The higher prices are offset by national trade-in subsidies of up to 140,000 yuan, sometimes topped up with local ones – in Hangzhou, Zhejiang, the total subsidy is 190,000 yuan, for instance.
New-energy HGV sales in China have been rising fast since 2022, when they had around 5 per cent of the market. Their market share had grown to 13.6 per cent by 2024 and reached 28.9 per cent in 2025, with sales of electric models up 182 per cent year on year. New-energy models accounted for 38.1 per cent of sales in the first nine months of 2026, closing in on the government’s 2030 target of 40 per cent four years ahead of time.
China has set 2030 as the target year for its carbon dioxide emissions to peak, as a first step to reaching carbon neutrality. By then, it also aims to have turned 20 per cent of its heavy-truck fleet electric. That means 1.6 million vehicles, up from 366,000 at the end of 2025.
A decarbonisation road map issued in May by 11 Chinese ministries designated transport as a priority sector for emissions cuts. The 8.6 million HGVs on the road in China at the end of 2025 – 2.3 per cent of all vehicles – accounted for nearly 40 per cent of its carbon emissions from transport, the Ministry of Transport said.
The plan calls for 30,000 kilometres of zero-carbon transport corridors by 2030.
Bigger, longer lasting, faster charging
Battery technology for HGVs in China has advanced on multiple tracks since 2020, when authorities began prioritising it.
The vehicles’ range – how far they can travel on a single charge – is being steadily extended by increasing battery density and efficiency. In September, CATL unveiled a heavy-truck battery with range of up to 1,000 kilometres, an improvement on the 800km of its predecessor.
CATL has developed a dual-battery set-up that further extends range. Electric HGV drivers typically maintain a buffer of 30 per cent of battery capacity in case of delays, detours and cold weather, which drains power faster. HGV batteries can be charged slowly or quickly depending on need. A low-power AC charger can be used for overnight charging at a depot, otherwise a DC fast charger is needed. High-wattage fast charging minimises downtime for drivers.

The roll-out of battery swapping has removed a barrier to the adoption of electric HGVs. Battery-powered HGVs are relatively easy to introduce because they exploit an existing energy system – the national electricity grid – whereas those powered by hydrogen fuel cells require building a new system, CleanTechnica, a renewable-energy news website, notes.

title_en: After Nvidia, will AMD be a target as China’s ‘2nd-choice’ supplier for AI chips?
content_en:
The sell-off was triggered by claims that AMD firmware was found in products from a Chinese server maker blacklisted by the US.
An AMD MI350 series AI chip is displayed at the San Jose McEnery Convention Center, in San Jose, California, June 12, 2025. Photo: Reuters
Short sellers have targeted Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) over alleged connections to Chinese firms blacklisted by Washington, erasing more than 10 per cent off its value in a matter of hours and fuelling speculation over whether it could be the next chip company in the crosshairs after Nvidia.
AMD shares plunged more than 7 per cent in regular trading on Thursday and slid another 3.4 per cent after hours, following a report from US investment firm Hunterbrook Capital disclosing a short position against the company.
The sell-off was triggered by claims from Hunterbrook Media – the firm’s affiliate outlet – that AMD firmware was found in products from IEIT Systems, a Chinese server maker under Inspur Group, which was blacklisted by the US Commerce Department in 2023, as well as three other companies with close ties to IEIT.
Hunterbrook alleged that AMD’s links to restricted entities left it “no less at risk from China chip restrictions than Nvidia”, warning that Washington could tighten curbs on its overseas business. However, the report did not establish that AMD violated US export controls.
AMD pushed back against the findings, telling CNBC and Bloomberg in a statement on Thursday that the report “misrepresented AMD’s business practices and relationships”. The company added that it “complies with applicable US export control laws and regulations and maintains rigorous processes to ensure compliance across our global operations”.
The Santa Clara, California-based chip designer did not immediately respond to a request for comment sent after normal US business hours.
The scrutiny of AMD comes just two days after rival Nvidia was targeted by prominent short sellers, including Muddy Waters and The Big Short trader Michael Burry. Until this week, AMD had been viewed by investors as a major beneficiary of Nvidia’s troubles, being the leading alternative supplier of graphics processing units (GPUs) amid tightening US export rules.
Adding to sector-wide jitters, the US House Foreign Affairs Committee on Thursday disclosed confidential licence applications from Chinese firms seeking to purchase advanced artificial intelligence processors from both Nvidia and AMD, specifically Nvidia’s H200 and AMD’s MI325X chips.
None of the approved shipments had been delivered as of May 11, according to the committee.
AMD’s exposure to possible China policy shifts could be larger than Nvidia’s, as 22.4 per cent of its revenue in 2025 came from mainland China and Hong Kong. Photo: Reuters
Who’s next?
As scrutiny widens across the global supply chain, chipmakers with larger revenue exposure to China – such as South Korea’s SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics, alongside US chip equipment maker Lam Research – could face heightened risk of becoming short-seller targets, according to Phelix Lee, a senior equity analyst at Morningstar.
Hunterbrook noted that AMD’s exposure to possible China policy shifts could be larger than Nvidia’s, as 22.4 per cent of its revenue in 2025 came from mainland China and Hong Kong, compared to 9 per cent for Nvidia.
Lee added that short-seller campaigns were often driven by short-term trading dynamics, making it difficult to predict which firm would be targeted next.
Laila Khawaja, head of research at consultancy Gavekal, said AMD’s status as the top alternative to Nvidia naturally put it under the microscope, given its opportunity to capture Chinese market share that Nvidia could no longer serve.
“AMD is certainly a potential target, although I think the stronger reason is its position as the second-choice supplier of advanced AI chips to China,” Khawaja said, while cautioning investors to “distinguish between legitimate questions about AMD’s China exposure and actual evidence of violations”.
Even so, AMD’s lower-key approach could help protect it from the political blowback facing Nvidia, whose former CEO Jensen Huang had publicly lobbied to expand chip sales to China, according to Lee.
“Despite China being a common geopolitical risk, how corporations communicate and react matters as much,” Lee said. “My impression is AMD has been quieter on chip sales lobbying, and there have been fewer chips tailored specifically for China.”
Additional reporting by Ben Jiang
By Iris Deng

title_en: China didn’t just host an Apec summit. It ran a year-long campaign
content_en:
Yalta was a world divided over a week. Shenzhen was something harder to read: a world reordered across a year.
Illustration: Mario Cameira
The image everyone will remember from Shenzhen is three men in one frame – Chinese President Xi Jinping, US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin, with Xi at the centre. But the story is not the smiling photos, or even the week. It is the 11 months that produced it. Beijing did not just host a summit. It ran a year-long campaign.
Since last December’s meeting opened the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum’s “China Year”, China has held three senior Apec officials’ meetings and 10 ministerial gatherings, with more than 300 events drawing more than 10,000 participants.
The West saw a photo opportunity. China was assembling an architecture.
The theme, “Building an Asia-Pacific Community to Prosper Together”, was set out in the Shenzhen Outlook declaration. In his keynote speech, Xi said Apec members were “like passengers riding the same ship”; cooperation was the refrain, the message discipline as deliberate as the seating chart. Pledges gave it weight – US$20 million for Apec cooperation, a new research centre and outcome documents on trade, connectivity and innovation.
[embedded media]
Consider the machinery. At the CEO summit on November 17-18, more than 2,000 gathered – 115 Fortune 500 companies, every Apec economy represented – with American firms forming the largest contingent at near 20 per cent. It issued the “Shenzhen Initiative”, the first initiative in the summit’s 30-year history.
The point: Beijing can convene the world’s capitals on its own calendar and stage.
Consider who got rewarded. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney arrived to find Beijing had lifted punitive tariffs on Canadian canola meal, peas, lobster and crab. Ottawa had done the same for Chinese electric vehicles earlier and hosted a yuan-denominated Chinese sovereign green bond in a North American first.
South Korean President Lee Jae Myung got the warm embrace: a third meeting with Xi in a year, the free trade pact’s second phase concluded – a courtship to keep Seoul leaning on Beijing for a reopening to the North even as Trump ties any meeting with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un to Xi. That is the relationship Tokyo wants to pull into its containment arc, and Beijing won’t let it go.
Consider who was left in the cold. Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi was kept at arm’s length – a handshake, a brief exchange, a second-row position. The Philippines, mired in South China Sea friction, got none of the favoured treatment. The sidelining was deliberate: you cannot elevate some without excluding others.
A group photo at the 33rd Apec Economic Leaders’ Meeting welcome banquet at the Shenzhen International Communication Centre in Guangdong province, China, on November 18. Photo: EPA
Beneath the hospitality, Beijing set out three tiers: the multilateral Apec floor of 21 economies, a middle band of bilateral meetings meted out as reward – or withheld – and, at the peak, the US-China-Russia trilateral meeting.
The tiers were worked across five dimensions. Security: the trilateral’s most concrete item, a push for norms governing artificial intelligence (AI) in nuclear command, with human control non-delegable. Economy: Shenzhen, the mainland’s first city to top 5 trillion yuan in trade, showcasing chips, robotics and the green industry. Technology: the AI dialogue began in September. Environment: statements touched on green technology and sustainable finance.
Finance was the quietest, most structural thread. It was also the connective tissue. Nearly a third of China’s trade is now settled in yuan, up 18 percentage points in a decade; the China-Russia share has jumped from 17 to 62 per cent in five years; more than 140 Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) institutions sit on China’s payments system.
It’s the old strategy of “encircling the cities from the countryside” – the Global South first, the rich later. It captures the year: build the base first, the glittering capital last.
[embedded media]
Which brings us to Thursday afternoon – the peak of the pyramid. Trump arrived weakened by a US midterm election defeat and left calling Xi a “friend”; Putin arrived to be told, gently, that he still matters. Xi arrived having spent a year as the indispensable node.
The three then issued a joint “declaration towards peace” – UN reform, stable energy, a curb on international courts and a pledge that a nuclear war “cannot be won and must never be fought” – with Xi trusting that “the seeds sown at [Shenzhen] will surely take root, sprout, blossom and bear fruit”. The trilateral was the smallest, most photographed tier – and, for Beijing, the capstone of the game.
Chinese President Xi Jinping at the meeting with US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin at Kylin Villa on November 19, in Shenzhen, China. Photo: Getty Images
This is what the power-politics reading gets backwards. It scans the room for a carve-up and finds three men posturing. But Beijing did not exercise leverage in the room; it accumulated it over the year, across every layer. China did not need to dominate the trilateral because it had already elevated itself across the region, sidelined critics, opened its market and deepened its currency’s reach.
None of this is settled. A year of staging cannot substitute for a convertible currency or a recovering property market, and Beijing knows it cannot afford to look all-powerful. Power politics has never required perfection – only a plan, a year and the discipline to let the world chase the spotlight while you build the stage.
Yalta was a world divided over a week. Shenzhen was something harder to read: a world reordered across a year, the decisive moves made not at the table everyone photographed but at the hundreds of others around it.
That, at least, is the bet behind the year-long effort – that when the trilateral spotlight fades, as it soon will, the architecture underneath outlasts it. Whether it does is a question only the years ahead can answer; the week in Shenzhen settled it for no one.
