title_display: China didn’t just host an Apec summit. It ran a year-long campaign
content_display:
Yalta was a world divided over a week. Shenzhen was something harder to read: a world reordered across a year.
Illustration: Mario Cameira
The image everyone will remember from Shenzhen is three men in one frame – Chinese President Xi Jinping, US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin, with Xi at the centre. But the story is not the smiling photos, or even the week. It is the 11 months that produced it. Beijing did not just host a summit. It ran a year-long campaign.
Since last December’s meeting opened the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum’s “China Year”, China has held three senior Apec officials’ meetings and 10 ministerial gatherings, with more than 300 events drawing more than 10,000 participants.
The West saw a photo opportunity. China was assembling an architecture.
The theme, “Building an Asia-Pacific Community to Prosper Together”, was set out in the Shenzhen Outlook declaration. In his keynote speech, Xi said Apec members were “like passengers riding the same ship”; cooperation was the refrain, the message discipline as deliberate as the seating chart. Pledges gave it weight – US$20 million for Apec cooperation, a new research centre and outcome documents on trade, connectivity and innovation.
[embedded media]
Consider the machinery. At the CEO summit on November 17-18, more than 2,000 gathered – 115 Fortune 500 companies, every Apec economy represented – with American firms forming the largest contingent at near 20 per cent. It issued the “Shenzhen Initiative”, the first initiative in the summit’s 30-year history.
The point: Beijing can convene the world’s capitals on its own calendar and stage.
Consider who got rewarded. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney arrived to find Beijing had lifted punitive tariffs on Canadian canola meal, peas, lobster and crab. Ottawa had done the same for Chinese electric vehicles earlier and hosted a yuan-denominated Chinese sovereign green bond in a North American first.
South Korean President Lee Jae Myung got the warm embrace: a third meeting with Xi in a year, the free trade pact’s second phase concluded – a courtship to keep Seoul leaning on Beijing for a reopening to the North even as Trump ties any meeting with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un to Xi. That is the relationship Tokyo wants to pull into its containment arc, and Beijing won’t let it go.
Consider who was left in the cold. Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi was kept at arm’s length – a handshake, a brief exchange, a second-row position. The Philippines, mired in South China Sea friction, got none of the favoured treatment. The sidelining was deliberate: you cannot elevate some without excluding others.
A group photo at the 33rd Apec Economic Leaders’ Meeting welcome banquet at the Shenzhen International Communication Centre in Guangdong province, China, on November 18. Photo: EPA
Beneath the hospitality, Beijing set out three tiers: the multilateral Apec floor of 21 economies, a middle band of bilateral meetings meted out as reward – or withheld – and, at the peak, the US-China-Russia trilateral meeting.
The tiers were worked across five dimensions. Security: the trilateral’s most concrete item, a push for norms governing artificial intelligence (AI) in nuclear command, with human control non-delegable. Economy: Shenzhen, the mainland’s first city to top 5 trillion yuan in trade, showcasing chips, robotics and the green industry. Technology: the AI dialogue began in September. Environment: statements touched on green technology and sustainable finance.
Finance was the quietest, most structural thread. It was also the connective tissue. Nearly a third of China’s trade is now settled in yuan, up 18 percentage points in a decade; the China-Russia share has jumped from 17 to 62 per cent in five years; more than 140 Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) institutions sit on China’s payments system.
It’s the old strategy of “encircling the cities from the countryside” – the Global South first, the rich later. It captures the year: build the base first, the glittering capital last.
[embedded media]
Which brings us to Thursday afternoon – the peak of the pyramid. Trump arrived weakened by a US midterm election defeat and left calling Xi a “friend”; Putin arrived to be told, gently, that he still matters. Xi arrived having spent a year as the indispensable node.
The three then issued a joint “declaration towards peace” – UN reform, stable energy, a curb on international courts and a pledge that a nuclear war “cannot be won and must never be fought” – with Xi trusting that “the seeds sown at [Shenzhen] will surely take root, sprout, blossom and bear fruit”. The trilateral was the smallest, most photographed tier – and, for Beijing, the capstone of the game.
Chinese President Xi Jinping at the meeting with US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin at Kylin Villa on November 19, in Shenzhen, China. Photo: Getty Images
This is what the power-politics reading gets backwards. It scans the room for a carve-up and finds three men posturing. But Beijing did not exercise leverage in the room; it accumulated it over the year, across every layer. China did not need to dominate the trilateral because it had already elevated itself across the region, sidelined critics, opened its market and deepened its currency’s reach.
None of this is settled. A year of staging cannot substitute for a convertible currency or a recovering property market, and Beijing knows it cannot afford to look all-powerful. Power politics has never required perfection – only a plan, a year and the discipline to let the world chase the spotlight while you build the stage.
Yalta was a world divided over a week. Shenzhen was something harder to read: a world reordered across a year, the decisive moves made not at the table everyone photographed but at the hundreds of others around it.
That, at least, is the bet behind the year-long effort – that when the trilateral spotlight fades, as it soon will, the architecture underneath outlasts it. Whether it does is a question only the years ahead can answer; the week in Shenzhen settled it for no one.

title_en: Hong Kong joins global drug body ahead of schedule, boosting regulatory ambitions
content_en:
Membership gives city a role in shaping international standards as it works towards independently assessing drugs and medical devices.
Lot Chan Sze-to, assistant director of health, left, alongside Li Zili, controller of medical products regulation; Ronald Lam Man-kin, director of health; and Frank Chan Ling-fung, assistant director of health, at a Department of Health press conference on Hong Kong’s admission to the International Council for Harmonisation. Photo: Emily Hung
Hong Kong has joined a global body for drug regulators ahead of schedule, a move health authorities say brings the city closer to establishing its own internationally recognised regulatory authority.
The city was admitted as the 20th regulatory member of the International Council for Harmonisation of Technical Requirements for Pharmaceuticals for Human Use (ICH) at an assembly meeting in Prague on Tuesday. It is poised to become a crucial “bridgehead” for mainland Chinese drugs to reach global markets amid current geopolitical tensions.
“After becoming an observer, it took us three years to become a regulatory member of the ICH, which is substantially faster than our original prediction of eight to 10 years. This showed that the SAR government has long attained top standards in drug and medical device regulation, and our determination in safeguarding public health,” Director of Health Ronald Lam Man-kin said at a press briefing on Friday.
The ICH is a non-profit organisation that brings together regulators and drug makers to harmonise technical requirements for the development and registration of safe, effective and high-quality medicines.
Since Hong Kong became an observer in 2023, health authorities have worked towards regulatory membership by attending meetings, appointing experts to ICH working groups and implementing its guidelines locally.
Lam attributed the rapid progress to the city’s strong regulatory foundations, as well as guidance and support from the National Medical Products Administration, the Hong Kong and Macau Affairs Office and the Chinese foreign ministry’s office in the city.
He said health authorities had also set up a task force to engage industry representatives and understand their regulatory needs.
Other ICH regulatory members include authorities from mainland China, Singapore, Switzerland, the United Kingdom and the United States.
Ronald Lam credits strong regulatory foundations and national support for Hong Kong’s early admission to a global drug body. Photo: Edmond So
“As a member of the ICH, we are now a player, a rule-maker and potentially a forerunner in international standards,” Lam said.
“Why are we becoming an international health and medical innovation hub? Because many innovative drugs will be able to access the mainland market through the drug regulatory regime of Hong Kong. Similarly, innovative drugs from the mainland could go global thanks to our international recognition.”
Authorities previously announced plans to introduce primary evaluation in phases by 2030, allowing Hong Kong to assess and approve drugs and medical devices independently, without relying on overseas approvals.
To facilitate that process, the government launched the 1+ mechanism in November 2023, allowing drug makers to seek registration in Hong Kong for products supported by local clinical data and approval from one foreign regulatory authority rather than two.
Lam said the government would not rule out bringing the 2030 timetable forward once the city had built up sufficient talent, expertise and experience, particularly for major innovative drugs to treat serious or rare conditions.
Since the first phase began in March this year, authorities have received five applications from mainland and overseas drug makers covering changes to therapeutic indications, dosages and product presentations.
Lam said 40 posts, including four at directorate level, would be added to the Centre for Medical Products Registration (CMPR), Hong Kong’s official drug regulator. These would be in addition to the Department of Health’s existing 420 regulatory affairs staff.
He added that Hong Kong joined the Pharmaceutical Inspection Co-operation Scheme (PIC/S) in 2016. The scheme focuses on setting standards for drug manufacturing and quality systems. According to its website, China applied for membership in 2023, but its application has yet to be approved.
Li Zili says common international standards help reduce duplication and synchronise drug development worldwide. Photo: Emily Hung
Controller for Medical Products Registration Li Zhili said ICH standards provided a common technical foundation that helped reduce duplication and synchronise drug development worldwide.
“Taking China and the United States as an example, with the reform of our country’s drug regulations and the ICH itself, the lag time [of a drug’s approval] between the two countries has substantially narrowed,” he said.
“Today, for some products and indications, approvals in China and the US are essentially granted simultaneously in many cases, and China sometimes even precedes the US. This not only reflects the achievements of China’s drug regulatory reforms but also the success of global drug development strategies and industry collaboration.”
Professor Alber Yu Cheung-hoi, founder and president of the Hong Kong Biotechnology Organisation, said ICH membership marked a milestone, strengthening the city’s credibility as a “bridgehead” for Chinese drugs entering global markets and overseas drugs reaching the mainland.
Yu said Hong Kong stood out among the 20 regulatory members, particularly for mainland companies, because the “certified in Hong Kong” label remained widely recognised and trusted despite current geopolitical tensions.
“If drugs are approved in Hong Kong, it might be easier for them to obtain approval elsewhere... it is the best stepping stone for mainland drugs,” he said.
He added that it was difficult to predict how many more drugs would be submitted for registration in Hong Kong, but many mainland drugmakers had expressed interest during talks he had given there.
“CMPR gives them one more way to prove that their drugs actually work. We couldn’t say Hong Kong is an easier way, but it is for sure a transparent one that gives them predictability and eases their worries,” he said.
By Emily Hung

title_en: Xi presses Trump to do ‘the right thing’ on Taiwan. Where does that leave US arms sales?
content_en:
Rather than halting deals, Beijing wants the US to limit them to existing types of defensive weapons, analyst says.
A US-made Patriot missile is launched during a live-fire exercise in Pingtung county, Taiwan in August 2024. Photo: AFP
Chinese President Xi Jinping urged visiting US President Donald Trump to do “the right thing” on Taiwan this week – a remark experts said suggested a push for further restrictions on US arms sales to the island.
“The US must keep doing the right thing to avoid major setbacks in China-US relations,” Xi told Trump during their bilateral talks on Thursday at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in Shenzhen, according to Beijing’s summary of the meeting.
Trump said the US did not support “Taiwan independence”, according to the same statement. The US has yet to release its own summary of the talks.
Ja Ian Chong, an associate professor of political science at the National University of Singapore, said Beijing’s statement appeared to call on Trump to “limit support for Taiwan”, which was consistent with previous requests.
“This could be a push from Xi for Trump to not approve further arms sales to Taiwan. Whether Trump wants to do so, or is able to do [so], as the new Congress comes in is an open question,” Chong said.
Under the 1979 Taiwan Relations Act (TRA), Washington is committed to supplying Taiwan with defensive weapons and maintaining the capacity to resist coercion against the island.
But the law leaves decisions on the nature and quantity of those weapons to the US Congress and president based on their assessment of Taiwan’s defence needs.
In a letter issued on Wednesday, just before Trump’s bilateral talks with Xi, nine Democratic US senators urged Trump to reaffirm the law “by sending US$14 billion in previously approved arms sales to Taiwan”. The deal was put on hold days before Trump’s May visit to Beijing.
[embedded media]
Experts said the delay was partly due to the political sensitivity of the deal, but also because of issues with production capacity. And with the Republicans losing control of both chambers of Congress in the US midterm elections, Trump could face new pressure over his Taiwan policy.
Chong said the US would continue to sell arms to the island “given the existence of the TRA and the view that Taiwan’s ability to defend itself reduces the probability of the United States or its allies getting involved in a conflict relating to Taiwan”.
Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited – by force if necessary. Most countries, including the United States, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.
Zhu Feng, dean of Nanjing University’s School of International Studies, noted that because the US had never stopped selling arms to the island, the prospect of Beijing persuading Washington to end the sales altogether was “virtually nonexistent”.
“What China wishes is that the types and the scale of the arms sales should be defensive weapons that have long existed, and the US can’t sell offensive weapons to Taiwan,” Zhu said.
He said Trump appeared to attach less strategic importance to Taiwan than his predecessor Joe Biden, but this did not mean there had been a fundamental change to Washington’s Taiwan policy.
Since last month, five US-made F-16V fighter jets have arrived in Taiwan as part of a US$7.76 billion package of 66 aircraft that Washington approved in August 2019.
By Albee Zhang

title_en: Vietnam scraps death sentence for drug trafficking
content_en:
The death sentence will only apply to four crimes: treason, murder, terrorism and illegal drug production.
Vietnamese policemen arrange seized methamphetamine at a police station in Ho Chi Minh City in 2019. Photo: AFP/Vietnam News Agency
Vietnam abolished the death penalty for drug trafficking and several other crimes on Friday, leaving execution available as a punishment for only four offences.
Communist Vietnam uses lethal injection as its execution method after retiring its firing squads in 2013, but has never made public the number of people it has put to death.
Amnesty International estimates more than 1,200 people were on death row in the country at the end of 2023.
In September, 11 people were condemned to die for trafficking drugs from France to Vietnam, according to media reports.
Under a revised penal code passed by the National Assembly on Friday, capital punishment would be available for only four crimes: treason, murder, terrorism and illegal drug production.
In addition to drug trafficking, the offences removed from the list included crimes against humanity, war crimes, rebellion and rape of a juvenile, with their maximum sentence replaced by life imprisonment.
It is the latest step in a long series of reductions since Vietnam’s 1985 penal code, which included the death penalty for 44 offences.
[embedded media]
Several national assembly deputies previously expressed reluctance to remove capital punishment for drug trafficking.
But Minister of Public Security Luong Tam Quang said evidence showed that several traffickers “had been lured, cheated or forced” into their actions.
“They can still be rehabilitated, educated and given the chance to make amends for their actions,” he said.
“So it’s not necessary to impose the death sentence.”
By Agence France-Presse

title_en: China’s rare earth magnet exports to US and EU fall after September rebound
content_en:
Japan buys 25 per cent more Chinese rare earth magnets despite diplomatic strains, bucking the broader monthly downturn in overseas sales.
Rare earth permanent magnets, used in many electric vehicle motors, remain a source of leverage for Beijing in trade talks with the EU and US. Photo: Reuters
China’s exports of rare earth permanent magnets to the US and the European Union resumed their decline in October, as Beijing navigated trade relations with both economies.
Exports to the US totalled 563.6 tonnes (621.26 short tonnes) last month, down 6.7 per cent from September, according to customs data released on Friday.
The decline reversed September’s 18 per cent month-on-month increase and left shipments 14.1 per cent lower than a year earlier.
Exports to the EU declined 9.7 per cent month on month to 2,216.5 tonnes. The drop followed a rebound in September, when shipments to the bloc reached their highest level since February.
The decline came as Beijing continued to engage with both the EU and the US on trade issues, holding talks with Brussels in early October over trade imbalances while preparing for a meeting between President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump on the sidelines of this week’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen.
Rare earth permanent magnets, essential to the production of hi-tech goods ranging from electric vehicles and smartphones to wind turbines, have remained a source of leverage for Beijing in trade negotiations with other economies, given China’s dominance in the sector.
China accounts for almost 95 per cent of permanent magnet production, according to the International Energy Agency.
[embedded media]
Following October’s trade negotiations with the EU, Beijing pledged to “continue to facilitate” export licence approvals for rare earths and permanent magnets destined for the EU through a “green channel”. The two sides also reached an understanding to cap Chinese hybrid car shipments to the bloc over the next four years.
The rare earth issue also looms large in China’s relations with Washington, as the US seeks to reduce its reliance on Chinese rare earth supplies and develop its own industry.
Earlier this week, Trump said the US would catch up with China in rare earths production “within 10 months”, claiming the US was “making rare earth at a level that we have never made before”. However, analysts have cautioned that such ambitions may be “unrealistic”, given China’s well-established and sophisticated rare earth supply chain, which has taken decades to develop.
Chinese exporters are required to obtain government approval before shipping certain permanent magnets overseas, following Beijing’s introduction of export controls on seven rare earth elements and related magnet materials in April last year, in response to US tariff hikes.
The US was China’s fourth-largest buyer of rare earth permanent magnets in October, after Germany, South Korea and India.
Exports to Japan, meanwhile, rose 25.1 per cent month on month to 214.6 tonnes, despite strained diplomatic ties between Beijing and Tokyo.
In total, China exported 5,694 tonnes of rare earth permanent magnets in October, a 7.6 per cent decline against September.
By Alice Li

[embedded media]
Following October’s trade negotiations with the EU, Beijing pledged to “continue to facilitate” export licence approvals for rare earths and permanent magnets destined for the EU through a “green channel”. The two sides also reached an understanding to cap Chinese hybrid car shipments to the bloc over the next four years.
The rare earth issue also looms large in China’s relations with Washington, as the US seeks to reduce its reliance on Chinese rare earth supplies and develop its own industry.
Earlier this week, Trump said the US would catch up with China in rare earths production “within 10 months”, claiming the US was “making rare earth at a level that we have never made before”. However, analysts have cautioned that such ambitions may be “unrealistic”, given China’s well-established and sophisticated rare earth supply chain, which has taken decades to develop.
Chinese exporters are required to obtain government approval before shipping certain permanent magnets overseas, following Beijing’s introduction of export controls on seven rare earth elements and related magnet materials in April last year, in response to US tariff hikes.
The US was China’s fourth-largest buyer of rare earth permanent magnets in October, after Germany, South Korea and India.
Exports to Japan, meanwhile, rose 25.1 per cent month on month to 214.6 tonnes, despite strained diplomatic ties between Beijing and Tokyo.
In total, China exported 5,694 tonnes of rare earth permanent magnets in October, a 7.6 per cent decline against September.

title_en: Evolution of China public holidays from ancient ‘golden weeks’ to modern make-up workdays
content_en:
Long breaks during the Song dynasty (960–1279) gave literati the freedom to travel and compose timeless poetry.
Festive decorations adorn Mojiaqiao Village in Hangzhou for Chinese New Year — part of a public holiday system China first introduced during the Han dynasty (202 BC–220). Photo: Xinhua/Xu Yu
Each year, when China releases its list of public holidays for the coming year, it sparks heated online discussions about the lack of days off – and sometimes even nostalgia for holidays in ancient China.
China first introduced statutory holidays during the Han dynasty (202 BC–220). Officials were required to live and work at their posts, but were allowed one day off every six days to rest and bathe.
Workers in China first had more flexible rotational leave systems during the Wei, Jin, Northern and Southern dynasties (220–589).
The Song dynasty (960–1279), considered the height of China’s ancient economy and civilisation, is believed to have offered the most holidays of any period in ancient China.
The government not only gave people time off for traditional festivals, but also established what might be called “golden weeks”: seven-day holidays for New Year’s Day and the Winter Solstice, and three-day holidays for the Lantern Festival, the Ghost Festival and the emperor’s birthday.
These long breaks gave literati such as Su Shi the chance to go on excursions and create timeless poetry.
Passengers are pictured at Hangzhou East Railway Station in east China’s Zhejiang province ahead of the Spring Festival, which typically sees the highest passenger traffic of the year. Photo by Long Wei/Xinhua
Another important form of leave during the Song dynasty was bereavement leave. As the dynasty placed great importance on filial piety, officials whose parents died were granted 100 days off.
However, given that journeys home could take days or even weeks, this leave was not necessarily as long as it seemed.
It is said that officials who lived far from home were also allowed to exclude travel time when calculating their leave.
The number of official holidays declined as imperial China gradually weakened. In the Ming dynasty (1368–1644), officials were given only one day off a month. In the Qing dynasty (1644–1912), apart from a month-long break around the turn of the year and about 20 days of festival holidays, officials were expected to work almost every day.
Moving forward to modern China, workers had only one day off a week until 1995, when the government officially introduced the two-day weekend.
However, many people still consider it a luxury to fully enjoy this policy today. Some companies give employees only one day off a week, effectively violating labour laws, often without facing legal consequences.
Visitors snap selfies at the Temple of Heaven (Tiantan) Park in Beijing during the National Day Golden Week, one of China’s major statutory holidays. Photo: Chen Xiaogen/Xinhua
Dissatisfaction with statutory holidays is also widespread among the public. China has only 13 days of paid statutory public holidays a year, spread across seven major festival periods. Even during the country’s most important festival, Chinese New Year, people are entitled to only four statutory days off.
In addition, to create longer “golden weeks”, the government often relies on compensatory workdays. Many people say this makes it seem as though they have more time off, but the weekends before and after the break are especially exhausting because they have to work to make up for the holidays.
Complaints about the lack of holidays and compensatory workdays continue to circulate online.
“I’m firmly against compensatory workdays. Why can’t they just increase the number of holidays?” one netizen asked.
“We may be expected to work long hours to drive economic growth, but having too few holidays doesn’t boost consumption,” another commented.

title_en: HKUST turns a 35-year-old vision into impact for the future of regional innovation
content_en:
University leaders reflect on how the institute has transformed itself into a major incubator for research and entrepreneurship in the region.
HKUST turns a 35-year-old vision into impact for the future of regional innovation
The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (HKUST) marks its 35th anniversary this year, having established itself as one of Asia’s most highly ranked universities with a reputation built around research excellence, entrepreneurship, innovation and national development. Behind this success is the vision of its founding president, the late Professor Woo Chia-wei.
“He didn’t just want to build a university,” says HKUST president Professor Nancy Ip Yuk-yu. “He envisioned an institution where education, research and innovation come together to create impact for society.”
Woo was also an early advocate of deeper integration between Hong Kong and mainland China, recognising the region’s potential as a hub for talent, research and innovation long before the Greater Bay Area entered public discourse.
HKUST council chairman Professor Harry Shum Heung-yeung says: “The concept of the Greater Bay Area was envisioned by our founding president, Professor Woo. He understood the importance of this area, not only for Hong Kong, but also for the future of the motherland.”
Guided by this vision, HKUST became one of the first Hong Kong universities to establish a research institute in Shenzhen in 1999. Today, that presence has evolved into an innovation network spanning Hong Kong, Shenzhen, Guangzhou, Foshan and Shanghai.
The foundation laid by Woo has enabled HKUST to build one of the region’s most vibrant research and innovation ecosystems. Under government-led initiatives, the university hosts seven InnoHK centres along with three State Key Laboratories to conduct frontier research in artificial intelligence (AI), semiconductors, robotics, renewable energy and biomedicine, with a strong focus on translating discoveries into real-world impact.
HKUST has nurtured an entrepreneurial culture, resulting in its giving birth to more than 2,000 start-ups, including 11 unicorns and 23 successful exits through initial public offerings as well as mergers and acquisitions. Among its most notable examples is drone technology company DJI, founded by HKUST alumnus Frank Wang.
Professor Nancy Ip (right), president of the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, brings a background in neuroscience to her role, while Professor Harry Shum, chairman of the university council, is a tech industry veteran and AI expert.
Looking ahead, Shum sees enormous potential in emerging fields such as the low-altitude economy – commercial activities that take place in airspace below 1,000 metres (3,281 feet) – and artificial intelligence. HKUST researchers with years of experience in developing these technologies, in addition to robotics, communications and autonomous systems, are contributing to the Hong Kong government’s low-altitude economy regulatory sandbox programme.
Shum also believes AI’s greatest promise lies in accelerating scientific discovery, transforming fields ranging from mathematics and materials science to drug development.
After 35 years, HKUST continues to champion cutting-edge research by translating bold scientific ideas into technological breakthroughs with real-world impact.
As it enters its next chapter, HKUST sees the Northern Metropolis, and particularly the development’s future San Tin University Town, as a natural extension of the institution’s founding mission. The megaproject across northern Hong Kong is designed to create housing, jobs and tech-driven growth alongside cross-border links with Shenzhen.
Central to this vision is the proposed establishment of Hong Kong’s third medical school. Ip believes the facility will offer an opportunity to pioneer a new model of medical education that draws on HKUST’s unique strengths in science, engineering, artificial intelligence and entrepreneurship.
“We envision a ‘closed-loop’ ecosystem where clinicians identify challenges at the bedside and work closely with scientists, engineers and industry partners to develop solutions. These innovations can then be brought back into the clinical setting to benefit patients,” she says.
HKUST has grown beyond its Clear Water Bay campus, expanding into mainland China with operations including a Guangzhou campus. Photo: SCMP/May Tse
She believes the Northern Metropolis can become a dynamic convergence point for talent, research, industry and healthcare innovation. “By integrating medicine, technology and entrepreneurship, we hope to nurture a new generation of clinician-scientists and innovators, while contributing to Hong Kong’s development as an international hub for medical and health innovation.”
Thirty-five years after its founding, HKUST remains guided by the vision that inspired its creation: advancing knowledge, nurturing talent and translating discovery into impact.

title_en: Mexican leader Sheinbaum’s 21-hour economy-class journey draws praise in China
content_en:
Social media users hail Claudia Sheinbaum’s ‘integrity and discipline’ for her choice of transport on the journey to the Apec summit.
After landing in Shenzhen, Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum took an airport shuttle bus to meet a welcoming party. Photo: Xinhua
Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum’s journey in economy class from Mexico City to Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit has gone viral on Chinese social media.
While most world leaders travelled to the southern Chinese city on chartered airliners or government aircraft, Sheinbaum arrived on Monday on a scheduled commercial flight.
She flew on China Southern Airlines flight CZ8032, according to CARNOC, a Chinese aviation trade publication.
The aircraft had a special blue, pink and yellow livery inspired by Guangdong, the province where Shenzhen is located. The design features the Hong Kong-Zhuhai-Macau Bridge and kapok flowers, which have been adopted as a symbol of the Greater Bay Area – the economic cluster linking Hong Kong, Macau and nine Guangdong cities.
Sheinbaum’s flight departed from Mexico City and stopped in Tijuana for around three hours before travelling on to Shenzhen. Including the stopover, the journey took around 21 hours in total.
Bloomberg reported that she had travelled in economy class, citing a diplomat familiar with the matter.
One Chinese social media user also said Sheinbaum had travelled in economy and posted pictures of her on board the plane.
Her trip drew praise on Chinese social media, with a hashtag about her arrival in Shenzhen gathering more than 10 million views.
The Mexican president was photographed on board the flight. Photo: Weibo
“A president with integrity and self-discipline,” read one comment.
“She deserves praise for saving taxpayers’ money and spending it where it matters, rather than on luxury jets and official travel,” another wrote.
Her predecessor, Andres Manuel Lopez Obrador, sold Mexico’s presidential plane at a loss to Tajikistan for US$92 million in 2023, saying it was costly to operate and maintain.
It cost about US$700,000 a year between February 2016 and July 2018, according to the Mexican newspaper Reforma – roughly 70 times Mexico’s annual gross domestic product per capita in those years.
The government said the proceeds from the sale helped fund two public hospitals in some of the poorest areas of southern Mexico.
Sheinbaum has pledged to uphold Lopez Obrador’s policy of “republican austerity” and ruled out having a presidential jet.
In the run-up to the summit, she said she was planning to take a commercial flight rather than a charter or military plane.
After landing, Sheinbaum took an airport shuttle bus to the red carpet, where she was welcomed by Chinese officials, an honour guard and children bearing flowers.
She then dined with some compatriots at a Mexican restaurant in Shenzhen, which also trended on Chinese social media.
[embedded media]
Sheinbaum had a face-to-face meeting with her Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping on Tuesday, which she described as “very cordial and collaborative”.
“I think it’s a very good opportunity to build even closer ties between Mexico and China,” she told reporters afterwards.
She added that the two sides discussed railway projects in Mexico, agriculture and smart hospitals, as well as ways to increase Mexican exports to China, according to a transcript released by the Mexican government.
Mexico is China’s second-largest trading partner in Latin America after Brazil, and bilateral trade has exceeded US$100 billion annually since 2023, according to Chinese state broadcaster CCTV.
By Eve Qiao

title_en: Malaysia plans to resettle 10,000 Rohingya in Turkey
content_en:
The refugees will undergo training in practical skills that are in demand in Turkey.
Rohingya refugees gather in front of the office of the UN Refugee Agency in Malaysia’s capital Kuala Lumpur, in July. Photo: Reuters
Malaysia is seeking to resettle 10,000 Rohingya migrants in Turkey as part of efforts to resolve a long-running refugee challenge involving foreign asylum seekers, the majority from Myanmar, a senior official said on Friday.
The announcement by Deputy Prime Minister Ahmad Zahid Hamidi comes a day after the UN’s top court, in a landmark ruling, said that Myanmar committed genocide against the ethnic minority.
“Following my recent official working visit to the Republic of Turkiye, the Cabinet has agreed to a proposal to resettle 10,000 Rohingya refugees from Malaysia to Turkiye through a structured skills training programme,” Ahmad Zahid said.
“I put forward this proposal as part of the government’s efforts to address the situation of Rohingya refugees in Malaysia in a more coordinated, effective and humane manner,” he said.
Rohingya refugees will undergo a Technical and Vocational Education and Training programme in Turkey which would last three to six months.
The training will focus on practical skills that are in demand among employers across various industries in Turkey, Ahmad Zahid said.
“With these skills, participants will be better equipped to secure employment and contribute to Turkiye’s economy, subject to the country’s rules and regulations,” Ahmad Zahid said in a statement.
A bus carrying Myanmar nationals being repatriated from Malaysia to their homeland, is seen on the outskirts of Kuala Lumpur on September 29. Photo: AFP
On Thursday, the International Court of Justice in The Hague, in its ruling, also ordered that refugees be given a safe passage home and awarded compensation.
Malaysia in late September repatriated about 1,500 Myanmar nationals under what authorities described as a voluntary programme, part of a scheme that rights groups warn could put migrants at risk by returning them to conflict-ridden Myanmar.
It was not immediately clear whether Rohingya refugees who would be selected for resettlement in Turkey would also participate on a voluntary basis.
Ahmad Zahid however, said the initiative “is in line with the principles that guide the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees in seeking lasting solutions for refugees”.
This included resettlement in a third country, “with due regard for their safety, protection and dignity”.
The Malaysian government said in October it would seek clarification from authorities in Myanmar over reports that hundreds of migrants recently returned to the country were being held in detention.
Rohingya, a persecuted mostly Muslim minority, make up two-thirds of the 190,000 Myanmar refugees and asylum seekers in Malaysia, according to the United Nations.
Malaysia, which shelters one of Southeast Asia’s biggest refugee populations, is not a signatory to the 1951 Refugee Convention and does not formally recognise their status.
By Agence France-Presse

title_en: Philippine military rejects Trump’s request for MacArthur-style gold baton
content_en:
The Philippines says the golden military baton is a one-off ‘historical symbol’ and is no longer part of the armed forces’ ranking system.
United States President Donald Trump (left) and Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr  toast during a luncheon at the Malacanang Palace in Manila on Wednesday. Photo: Reuters
The Philippine military has clarified that a gold baton awarded to the late American general Douglas MacArthur is no longer part of its honours system, dampening a demand for a similar accolade from US President Donald Trump.
Addressing a state lunch gathering at the presidential palace in Manila on Wednesday, Trump paid tribute to the long-standing diplomatic relations between the two countries.
“From William Howard Taft to Dwight D. Eisenhower, some of the best minds and foremost leaders of our nation, that our nation has ever produced … They always knew that this was a place of great potential,” he said.
Trump’s praise for his hosts was followed by an unusual wish: for the Philippine government to repeat its 1936 act by bestowing a golden military baton on him, like the one MacArthur received from former leader Manuel L. Quezon.
“Of course, it was right here, this very palace, that president Quezon bestowed Douglas MacArthur with a gold baton and the rank of field marshal in the Philippine army,” Trump said. “I’d like to have you do that to me, if you don’t mind. I’d love that. Why the hell shouldn’t I get that?”
The gold baton the Philippines presented to Douglas MacArthur is displayed in a museum dedicated to the late general in Norfolk, Virginia. Photo: Facebook/macarthurmemorial
Quezon also granted MacArthur the rank of field marshal in the Philippine military – the only such designation in the country’s history – to help build its armed forces.
Trump, who was in Manila to attend the Asean summit, also announced at the banquet attended by President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr that the United States had sealed a “very big trade deal” with the Philippines.
But his desire appeared destined to be unfulfilled after the army said the position of field marshal and its baton were not carried over into the succeeding rank structure and were no longer part of the armed forces.
“This distinction was given as part of MacArthur’s duties as military adviser to the Commonwealth government in organising and developing the Philippine army,” it said in a statement on Thursday.
It added that the “baton remains a historical symbol” of the military’s heritage and the long-standing defence ties between the Philippines and the US, ABS-CBN reported.
General Douglas MacArthur wades ashore during the Allies’ initial landings at Leyte Island in the Philippines in October 1944. Photo: US National Archives
MacArthur, who served as supreme commander of the Southwest Pacific during the second world war, was a venerated figure in the Philippines. The Manila Hotel has a MacArthur Suite and a park in Leyte hosts a life-size bronze statue of him.
He once famously said: “Give me 10,000 Filipinos, and I shall conquer the world.”
When he was forced to evacuate to Australia after Japanese troops overwhelmed American and Philippine forces in 1942, he vowed to return – and did just that two years later, wading ashore on Leyte Island alongside Allied troops.
That moment was reenacted in 1994 by American actor Ken Metcalfe, Philippine stars Ernie Zarate and Hernan Robles, and a group of other professional entertainers, who walked through the surf in front of thousands of spectators in Leyte.
The general’s life was also chronicled in the 1977 war drama MacArthur, starring Oscar-winning actor Gregory Peck.
US President Donald Trump responds to a question from the media in the Oval Office of the White House on November 5. Photo: EPA
Trump’s penchant for gold has sparkled throughout most of his political and business life. Many of his residential and commercial buildings feature golden decor.
He renovated the Oval Office at the White House with gilded interiors including gold-painted carvings and glittering carpeting. During the midterms campaign last month, former president Barack Obama joked that Trump’s decor style made the presidential office look like “Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory”.
When Trump visited South Korea last year, President Lee Jae Myung capitalised on his affinity for flattery diplomacy and presented his US counterpart with a gold crown. An elated Trump quipped: “I’d like to wear it right now.”

title_en: Is China’s 195km pure hydrogen pipeline a clean energy breakthrough?
content_en:
The project in Inner Mongolia could address one of the biggest challenges facing wider adoption, according to state media.
A green hydrogen transportation station in Kundulun district, Baotou, north China’s Inner Mongolia autonomous region. Photo: Xinhua
China’s first long-distance pipeline dedicated to transporting pure hydrogen over more than 100km (62 miles) has begun operations, in a development that could help lower the cost of delivering the clean energy source to users.
The 195km (121-mile) pipeline in the industrial city of Baotou, north China’s Inner Mongolia autonomous region, was selected by the National Energy Administration as part of an initial batch of hydrogen-energy pilot projects, state news agency Xinhua reported on Thursday.
Hydrogen storage and transport have long posed obstacles to expanding its use, as moving the gas by road over long distances can be prohibitively expensive. Pipelines could lower delivery costs, fuelling the push to develop such infrastructure, according to the report.
Building pure hydrogen pipelines posed challenges, however, and China’s network had “long been in the exploratory and development stage”, it added.
“This project marks a key breakthrough in China’s large-scale, long-distance pure hydrogen pipeline transport, promoting the coordinated development of the entire green hydrogen industry chain from production to storage, transportation and use,” the Xinhua report stated.
Wider use of hydrogen could help China reduce emissions in industries such as steelmaking and aviation, where alternatives to fossil fuels were limited, according to an earlier state media report published on the Chinese government’s website.
“From a policy perspective, from a government support perspective, I don’t find it so surprising that they’re using hydrogen,” said Alfredo Montufar-Helu, China-based managing director at Ankura Consulting. “Hydrogen, from what I’ve heard, is not an easy resource to manage. It’s volatile.”
Montufar-Helu said he had not previously heard of a pipeline in China designed to transport hydrogen over long distances. “Is it a breakthrough? Probably,” he said.
China’s experience of building long pipelines could give it the “potential” to incorporate hydrogen into wider green-energy plans, he added.
The project is run by a Baotou subsidiary of China Huadian, a state-owned power generator. It is expected to support an annual green hydrogen production capacity of 7,800 tonnes, supplying users in the chemical, metallurgical, gas and transportation sectors, Xinhua reported.
Inner Mongolia has abundant wind and solar resources, making it well suited to producing green hydrogen. The energy source produces water rather than carbon dioxide when burned or used in a fuel cell.
Wang Xinyu, director of pipeline builder Inner Mongolia Huadian Hydrogen Energy Technology, said the infrastructure had an approved annual transport capacity of 100,000 tonnes (110,231 short tons). Transporting green hydrogen could cost as little as 3 yuan (44 US cents) per kilogram, Wang said, according to Xinhua.
